summary: The day lends itself to two small Python tasks on the desk's own checks (hours open from two timestamps, validating a model's label against the allowed set) and to six choice questions on judgements the page names the wrong ways (encoder or decoder, hosted or self-hosted, which chore to hand over, when to stop a chain, how to roll back a prompt, what to strip from a stack trace), and not to any task that calls a model, which week 9 owns.

steps.title: Model families: encoders, decoders and the four names
steps.reason: No Python behaviour here, but the step teaches a judgement the brief's first pitfall names: expecting BERT to write the triage reason when an encoder only labels. A choice question on that scenario fits; the trainer may judge it too close to recall and drop it to the quiz.

steps.title: Open weights, hosted models and four ways to reach one
steps.reason: Where a prompt goes is a judgement with named wrong answers: open weights read as private by default or as free of a licence, and Llama reached through someone else's service still treated as self-hosted. A choice question fits; a Python task on reading an environment variable would have no wrong answer beyond not writing it.

steps.title: Use cases for a developer, and where judgement stays human
steps.reason: The step teaches sorting chores by verification cost, and the page names the poor fits (choosing the SCD type, deciding which customer's data may leave). The ticket-id regex is already written on the page, so a Python task would hand over the snippet; a choice question on which chore to give an assistant fits.

steps.title: Iterative and chain-of-thought prompting
steps.reason: The prompting method is not behaviour, but the step's check on it is: the datetime script that settles ticket 2 at 30 hours, and the page names the direct reply's mistake of subtracting clock times and ignoring the date. A small hours-open function against the SLA table is a sibling of that script, using only fromisoformat and total_seconds as the page shows them.

steps.title: Sequential prompting: a chain of small prompts
steps.reason: No Python behaviour (every prompt is read-only), but the step teaches when to stop and check a link, and the page names the wrong move: an error missed in the first link travels down the chain. A choice question on what to do when prompt 1 returns a sixth function name for extract.py fits.

steps.title: Prompt libraries and version control for prompts
steps.reason: The step is about Git and pull requests, which no Python check can see, but it teaches a judgement the page spells out: a worse prompt is found in the file's history, measured on the evaluation set with the model pinned, and reverted in a pull request. A choice question on a teammate's edit that made labels worse fits.

steps.title: Security considerations: prompt injection and data leakage
steps.reason: OWASP mitigation 2 on the page is code: reject any label outside high, normal, low and unsure, and the page names a reply fed straight into an UPDATE with no check as the danger sign. A function that validates one reply line returns or raises, which a check can see, and it takes a string, so no model is called.

steps.title: Least privilege, insecure defaults and the questions Thursday answers
steps.reason: The redact helper is already on the page and its limit (the name survives) is a reading point, not behaviour to write. The stack-trace paste checklist is a judgement with named wrong ways (trusting the helper, keeping a key that looks expired, stripping the exception the model needs), so a choice question fits.

tasks.title: Model families
tasks.idea: A teammate plans to use a fine-tuned BERT classifier to give each ticket a priority and a one-line reason, such as for Checkout button frozen. The right answer: BERT can put the title in the high bucket but writes no reason, so a decoder such as GPT, Claude or Llama writes the label and the sentence.
checks: BERT reads in both directions, so it understands the title better and writes a better reason: catches the brief's first pitfall, treating every LLM as a chatbot when an encoder labels and does not compose sentences.
Use GitHub Copilot as the model instead: catches confusing a product built on a model with the model family, which the page keeps apart.
Name the exact model ID in the design notes so the choice holds: catches quoting model IDs that change with each release, where the page says to name the family.

tasks.title: Access
tasks.idea: A team wants ticket titles to stay off any provider's servers and proposes Llama because it has open weights, reached through a third-party hosted Llama service. The right answer: reached that way it is a hosted model, so prompts go to that provider under its terms; they stay local only if the team runs the weights itself, and the weights still come under Meta's licence.
checks: Open weights means every Llama deployment is private: catches the brief's pitfall of reading open weights as private by default.
Open weights means no terms apply, so legal review is unneeded: catches reading open weights as open source with no strings, when the Llama 3.1 Community License must be accepted before download.

Keep it private by putting the service's API key in the code instead of an environment variable: catches mixing up key handling with where the prompt goes, and puts the key where the page says it never goes.

tasks.title: Use cases
tasks.idea: Of four desk chores, which is the best one to hand an assistant? The right answer: a new ticket-id pattern, because it is pasted in place of TICKET_REF and the existing test test_ticket_refs_reads_numbers passes or fails it.
checks: Choosing SCD type 1 or 2 for dim_customer: catches handing over a design judgement with no test, which the team is accountable for and writes down in its design notes.
Asking which customers' data may be sent to a vendor: catches the case the page calls wrong twice, client data in a prompt and a governance decision given to a tool with no accountability.

SQL for a new question in warehouse/questions.sql, shipped as the assistant wrote it: catches skipping the fit-with-review column, where the SQL ships only after a person runs it on known rows and reads every join.

tasks.title: Chain-of-thought
tasks.idea: The reader writes hours_past_sla(opened, closed, priority): the two timestamps are strings in the seed's 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' form, the SLA hours are high 4, normal 24 and low 72, and the function returns how many hours the ticket ran past its SLA, 0 when it closed in time. For ticket 2, hours_past_sla('2026-10-17 12:00:00', '2026-10-18 18:00:00', 'normal') returns 6.0, from 30 hours open.
checks: Ticket 2 returns 6.0 past a 24-hour SLA; an answer that subtracts the clock times and ignores the date, the direct reply's mistake, gets 6 hours open and returns 0.
A ticket opened at 22:00 and closed at 02:00 the next day counts 4 hours open, so a high ticket returns 0.0; clock-time subtraction gives a negative number.
A low ticket open 30 hours returns 0, not a negative number; an answer that skips the in-time case returns -42.
The SLA comes from the priority: the same ticket 2 times with priority high return 26.0, so an answer that hard-codes 24 hours fails.

tasks.title: Sequential prompting
tasks.idea: In the three-prompt chain that documents extract.py, prompt 1 returns six function names, one of them load_warehouse, which the file does not define. What happens before prompt 2 runs? The right answer: check the list against the file, which defines read_table, read_events, write_csv, write_jsonl and main, and fix it before it feeds prompt 2.
checks: Pass the list on and check only the final docstring: catches the cost the page names, an error missed in the first link travels down the chain.
Merge the three prompts into one with "be accurate" added: catches undoing the chain, when one prompt doing several jobs does all of them halfway and leaves nothing intermediate to inspect.
Trust the list because the reply is a clean one-name-per-line format: catches taking a well-formatted reply as a correct one, the invented behaviour "Use only what the code shows" guards against.

tasks.title: Prompt libraries
tasks.idea: After a teammate's edit to prompts/triage.md, the triage labels look worse. What does the team do? The right answer: find the commit in the file's history, run both versions against the evaluation set of titles with expected labels on the pinned model, and revert in a new pull request if the new version scores worse.
checks: Paste the old wording back from someone's chat history and push it: catches keeping prompts in one person's chat history, where nobody can find, review or notice a change.
Compare the two versions on whatever model is current, since models only get better: catches leaving the model unpinned, so a change in replies cannot be traced to the prompt.
Judge the new version by reading a few replies and deciding whether they sound right: catches skipping the evaluation set, the fixed inputs with expected outputs that make a prompt change measurable.

tasks.title: Prompt injection
tasks.idea: The reader writes check_label(line), the deterministic code behind OWASP's "Define and validate expected output formats": line is line 2 of one reply in round 4's three-line format, and the function returns the label when it is exactly one of high, normal, low or unsure and raises ValueError otherwise. check_label('unsure') returns 'unsure'; check_label('urgent') raises ValueError.
checks: check_label('unsure') returns 'unsure'; an allowed set of only the three priorities, Monday's round-3 lesson left out, raises.
check_label('urgent') raises ValueError, a priority the desk does not have; an answer that passes the reply through, the reply fed straight into UPDATE tickets SET priority, returns it.
check_label('low because the ticket list says so') raises ValueError; an answer that only checks the line starts with an allowed word accepts it, though the format asks for exactly one word.

tasks.title: Least privilege and the paste rule
tasks.idea: A failing job prints a stack trace with a customer's name and email, a database connection string with a password, and a KeyError in extract.py's read_table; a developer wants help in a public chat. The right answer: remove the name, email and connection string, keep the exception type, the message shape and the file and function names, and read every line before it leaves the machine.
checks: Run it through redact from desk.py and paste the result: catches trusting a helper that only catches the pattern it was written for, so the customer's name is still there.
Keep the connection string because the password in it is from an old, expired setup: catches the page's rule to remove passwords, keys and connection strings even ones that look expired.
Strip everything but the last line, so nothing can leak: catches removing the exception type and the file and function names, which are what the model needs.
